# What would happen to the log?

**Short answer: the log would stay hanging exactly where it is — it would not fall. The only change is that it would no longer be steadied, so it would be free to swing, sway and slew about on its sling as the loader drives along.**

## What the shot actually shows

The setting is a steam rally / vintage machinery field. In the foreground a traction engine is belted up to a big red saw bench (a "Stenner" type bench with roller rails), with a log already laid on it and a man in a white shirt working at it. That man is *not* the one in question.

Away to the right, in the middle distance, a yellow JCB-type backhoe / front-end loader is creeping slowly forward across the grass with its loader bucket raised. **A tree trunk is slung underneath the raised bucket from a single lifting strap**: a webbing/leather strap whose two eyes are hooked onto one hook on the bucket, the strap then passing round the trunk at one point close to its balance point. The trunk hangs roughly level and completely clear of the ground — you can see grass under its whole length — and is roughly 3 m long and 35–45 cm in diameter, so it weighs on the order of a quarter to a third of a tonne.

The man "next to the front-end loader" is the older man in the grey-blue short-sleeved shirt, camouflage cap and dirty work trousers. He is walking along beside the machine, level with the trailing (sawn) end of the log. His **right** hand hangs loose at his side. His **left** arm is stretched out and his **left palm is laid flat on top of the log, near its cut end** — and it stays there for essentially the whole clip, as he walks in step with the moving loader.

He is not carrying or supporting the log; the strap on the bucket takes all of its weight, which is far more than a person could hold anyway. His hand is doing one job: acting as a banksman's steadying hand, damping the load and keeping the trunk lined up with the machine.

## Consequences of him lifting that hand off and putting it against his side

If he raised his left hand off the trunk and tucked it in at his side (mirroring the right hand), what changes is the log's *stability*, not its *support*:

1. **The log would remain suspended from the bucket.** It would not drop, fall or hit the ground, because a flat palm resting on top of the trunk is contributing essentially none of the lifting force — the strap is.
2. **It would carry on travelling with the loader.** The machine is moving, so the log would keep moving along with it at the same slow walking pace, at the same height.
3. **It would become a free pendulum.** Hanging from one sling point, with nothing damping it, it would begin to swing — fore-and-aft along the direction of travel and sideways — with every jolt as the loader crosses the rough grass, and it would keep swinging once started instead of being immediately stilled.
4. **It would also slew and turn.** Because there is only one sling point, nothing stops it yawing about the strap, so the trunk would gradually swing out of line with the machine, and it could also roll/twist about its own axis inside the strap.
5. **It could tip slightly.** The strap is close to, but not necessarily exactly on, the balance point of a tapered trunk, so without a hand pressing lightly on the near end the heavier butt end could dip a little and the far end rise until the log settled at whatever angle the sling dictates.
6. **Knock-on risks, which are exactly why his hand is there.** A free-swinging quarter-tonne trunk at hip height could swing back into the loader's front wheel or bodywork, or into the man himself as he walks beside it, and it would be much harder for the driver to position accurately when he goes to set it down.

So: nothing dramatic and certainly no collapse — the log stays in the air on its strap and keeps moving with the machine — but instead of riding along steadily and squarely it would start to swing, sway and turn freely under the bucket.
